paper: 3D Bioprinter Firmware Attacks: Categorization, Implementation, and Impacts
attacks_mentioned: Firmware-based IP/data theft, persistent bootloader compromise (MalBoot), printer hardware sabotage, temperature manipulation, print-speed alteration, nozzle switching, contamination risks, and standoff-distance manipulation
lifecycle_stage: Firmware compromise during build execution; post-print quality and cell-viability assessment.
purdue_level: L1 firmware and bootloader; L0 printer hardware
threat_model: Supply-chain adversary has physical device access and access to firmware/bootloader source, enabling malicious firmware installation and persistence, with data theft and device/construct sabotage objectives.

paper: 3D Printer Audio and Vibration Side Channel Dataset for Vulnerability Research in Additive Manufacturing Security
attacks_mentioned: Acoustic and vibration side-channel attacks potentially enabling reconstruction of printing movements, design information theft, and counterfeiting.
lifecycle_stage: Side-channel information leakage during printing.
purdue_level: L0 printer motion, audio/vibration emissions and sensors; process signals may disclose L1 motion behavior.
threat_model: Dataset supports study of IP leakage from acoustic/vibration measurements using nearby iPhone or Teensy sensors; no particular adversary, access policy or successful reconstruction is established.

paper: A Blockchain-Based G-Code Protection Approach for Cyber-Physical Security in Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Malicious G-code/design modifications, unauthorized toolpath manipulation, and intellectual property theft through G-code access.
lifecycle_stage: G-code generation, storage, secure transfer, and protection before build execution.
purdue_level: L3 preparation/storage of G-code; blockchain data storage may be L5–L4

paper: A correlation among industry 4.0, additive manufacturing, and topology optimization: a state-of-the-art review
venue: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology; 2023
attacks_mentioned: General AM cybersecurity threats, data-privacy risks, IP protection concerns, and supply-chain cyberattack risks. No specific attack is experimentally demonstrated.
lifecycle_stage: Primarily digital design/optimization and connected manufacturing processes.
purdue_level: L3 design/topology optimization and build preparation; L2–L0 connected equipment and physical manufacturing
threat_model: Surveys Industry 4.0, topology optimization and AM

paper: Acoustic Side-Channel Attacks on Additive Manufacturing Systems
attacks_mentioned: Side-channel -> Acoustic attack
lifecycle_stage: Side-channel information leakage during printing.
purdue_level: L0 stepper motors, motion and acoustic emissions, disclosing information about L1 printer control.
threat_model: Acoustic eavesdropper uses a nearby microphone and trained signal-learning models to infer movement axes, distance and G-code for IP reconstruction; no control of printer is required.

paper: A cyber-physical attack taxonomy for production systems: a quality control perspective
attacks_mentioned: IP theft, equipment sabotage, product dimensional manipulation, mechanical-property alteration, and attacks designed to evade quality-control (QC) systems.
lifecycle_stage: Production execution and quality inspection. Applicable to manufacturing broadly, not exclusively AM.
purdue_level: L2 quality-control monitoring and L1–L0 production equipment.
threat_model: Taxonomy analyzes attacker objective, access, location and effect in production/QC systems

paper: A Data Exfiltration and Remote Exploitation Attack on Consumer 3D Printers
venue: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security; 2016
attacks_mentioned: Unauthorized extraction of stored print files, remote printer manipulation, exploitation of unauthenticated web services and flawed TLS implementations.
lifecycle_stage: Printer communication, stored print jobs, and remote machine control.
purdue_level: L2 network-facing printer services, authentication and stored jobs; physical printer at L0 is downstream of remote control.
threat_model: Attacker has ordinary client-level access to the same network but no elevated network privileges or physical access. They seek authentication codes and tokens to exfiltrate stored object data or remotely manipulate MakerBot printers.

paper: Additive Manufacturing Cyber-Physical System: Supply Chain Cybersecurity and Risks
attacks_mentioned: Design theft and modification, malware, ransomware, side-channel attacks, printer-parameter sabotage, raw-material tampering, reverse engineering, and counterfeit production.
lifecycle_stage: Digital preparation, material supply, build execution, and product authentication.
purdue_level: L5–L4 enterprise/supply-chain data, L3 digital preparation and L1–L0 machine/material handling
threat_model: Supply-chain analysis surveys attacks on design information, raw materials and printer hardware. Threat actors and access vary by the digital, material and hardware chain; no single attacker model.

paper: An LSTM-Autoencoder Based Online Side Channel Monitoring Approach for Cyber-Physical Attack Detection in Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Malicious alterations to printed-part geometry and layer thickness.
lifecycle_stage: In-situ monitoring during build execution.
purdue_level: L0 FFF machine vibrations and accelerometers; L2 supervisory online monitoring and anomaly analysis.
threat_model: Two experimental process alterations mimic compromised part geometry and layer thickness on an FFF machine

paper: A Non-Line-of-Sight, Multi-Modality-based Side-Channel IP Theft Attack on Additive Manufacturing Using Dual Smartphones
attacks_mentioned: Side-channel IP theft through acoustic and magnetic emissions, enabling unauthorized G-code reconstruction without direct printer access.
lifecycle_stage: Information leakage during active printing
purdue_level: L0 printer physical emissions observed externally, disclosing aspects of L1 motion commands.
threat_model: An eavesdropper positions two smartphones 60 cm away without line of sight, recording acoustic and magnetic emissions to reconstruct G-code and steal design IP.

paper: An Online Side Channel Monitoring Approach for Cyber-Physical Attack Detection of Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Malicious part-geometry modifications and layer-thickness alterations.
lifecycle_stage: In-situ attack monitoring during build execution.

paper: A Novel Hierarchical Security Solution for Controller-Area-Network-Based 3D Printing in a Post-Quantum World
attacks_mentioned: CAN message manipulation, eavesdropping, replay attacks, device impersonation, hardware Trojans, fuzzing, and denial-of-service attacks.
lifecycle_stage: Printer-controller communications and execution-time network security.
purdue_level: L1 CAN devices, routing and controller communication; L0 connected printer sensors and actuators; L2 supervisory root when deployed.
threat_model: Addresses malicious CAN-node traffic and hardware Trojans that may eavesdrop, spoof, replay, fuzz, impersonate or disrupt printer communications; architecture isolates affected subnets and assumes authentication/key mechanisms.

paper: A Physical Hash for Preventing and Detecting Cyber-Physical Attacks in Additive Manufacturing Systems
attacks_mentioned: STL file manipulation, toolpath modification, process-parameter tampering, and intellectual property theft.
lifecycle_stage: Protection of build specifications and verification during build execution.
purdue_level: L3 geometry/toolpath preparation and hash specification; L0 printing, camera and physical QR code; L2 independent monitoring/inspection.
threat_model: Adversary alters the STL, toolpath or process parameters; defense assumes an air-gapped measurement system and trusted designer-specified hash and parameter ranges.

paper: A review on machine learning in 3D printing: applications, potential, and challenges
attacks_mentioned: Cybersecurity risks associated with AM and cloud-based manufacturing are included as a review topic;
lifecycle_stage: Design and process optimization, manufacturing monitoring, and quality assessment.
purdue_level: L3 design/optimization, L2 monitoring analytics, and L0 physical quality measurements;
threat_model: Reviews machine-learning uses including attack detection for 3D printing; cited attacks

paper: Assessing the Cybersecurity of Connected 3D Printers Using Large Language Models (LLMs)
attacks_mentioned: Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks, malicious G-code modification, and unauthorized manipulation of printing instructions.
lifecycle_stage: G-code preparation, transmission, and build execution.
purdue_level: L3 Cura/G-code preparation, L2 networked host/printer interface, L1–L0 printer execution and resulting part.
threat_model: Assumes adversary has network access and knows the printer IP, using ARP spoofing and packet capture to intercept and manipulate G-code between Cura host and Ultimaker S5.

paper: A Survey of Cybersecurity of Digital Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: IP theft, design and G-code tampering, reverse engineering, side-channel leakage, covert-channel attacks, denial-of-service, product sabotage, and counterfeiting.
lifecycle_stage: Digital authorization, design/toolpath preparation, manufacturing execution, and product authentication.
purdue_level: L5–L4 enterprise, L3 manufacturing engineering and L2–L0 control/physical equipment across surveyed workflows.
threat_model: Digital-manufacturing survey discusses multiple adversary objectives and attack techniques; capabilities/access depend on cited cases rather than one new model.

paper: A Survey on Limitation, Security and Privacy Issues on Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Firmware manipulation, G-code tampering, side-channel IP theft, unauthorized printer access, design sabotage, sensor manipulation, material contamination, and equipment damage.
lifecycle_stage: Access control and design protection, manufacturing execution, and verification of printed components.
purdue_level: L5 access/authentication and design exchange, L3 build preparation, L2–L0 device/control/physical process as discussed across cited cases.
threat_model: Surveys diverse AM security/privacy attacks and authentication mechanisms;

paper: Attack-Defense Modeling of Material Extrusion Additive Manufacturing Systems
venue: Critical Infrastructure Protection XVI (IFIP Advances in Information and Communication Technology, vol. 666); 2022
attacks_mentioned: Cyberattacks targeting design, slicing, and printing processes; four case-study attacks involving identified system vulnerabilities and developed exploits.
lifecycle_stage: Digital-design handling, slicing, and printing execution.
purdue_level: L3 design and slicing tools, L2 printer interfaces, L1 firmware/controllers and L0 printing process as affected by the specific case studies.
threat_model: Attack-defense analysis models design, slicing and printing attack vectors and reports four attacks on three printers; attacker access/capabilities differ by case rather than one global adversary.

paper: A Voxel-Based Watermarking Scheme for Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Unauthorized modification, copying, distribution, and reproduction of digital models, G-code, and printed objects; intellectual property infringement.
lifecycle_stage: Digital-model preparation, G-code generation and printing, and physical-part authentication.
purdue_level: L3 voxel model watermarking and G-code preparation; L0 manufactured specimen and physical readout.
threat_model: Considers infringement and unauthorized copying of digital designs and printed parts; watermark decoding requires knowledge of the chosen encoding/view parameters, while a systematic adversarial removal trial is not established.

paper: BioSaFe: Bioprinting Security Framework for Detecting Sabotage Attacks on Printability and Cell Viability
attacks_mentioned: Six sabotage attacks: nozzle switching, UV curing manipulation, thermodynamic/temperature manipulation, Z-profile (layer-height) manipulation, Quick Pause in Print (QPIP), and contamination through filtration-system manipulation.
lifecycle_stage: Build execution, UV curing, and post-print quality assessment.
purdue_level: L3 trusted build instructions; L2 monitoring; L1 printer control; L0 sensors, extrusion and cell-bearing construct.
threat_model: Assumes adversary can manipulate bioprinting parameters/process to sabotage printability or cell viability; monitoring compares measured behavior with trusted instructions. Exact initial compromise is not established here.

paper: Blockchain-Based IoT Integration for VAT Photopolymerization Additive Manufacturing Process Security and Transparency
attacks_mentioned: Potential unauthorized access, manipulation, and integrity compromise of IoT sensor data, particularly volatile organic compound (VOC) monitoring records. No specific cyberattack experimentally demonstrated.
lifecycle_stage: Manufacturing-process monitoring and traceable environmental compliance records.
purdue_level: L0 VOC/environment sensors, L2 monitoring and L5 enterprise/blockchain access controls and records; deployment architecture is inferred.
threat_model: Threats include unauthorized modification/access to IoT process/environment records; the paper does not establish a demonstrated attack or precise adversary access.

paper: Blockchain-Based Quality Management for a Digital Additive Manufacturing Part Record
attacks_mentioned: Potential tampering with manufacturing and quality records, unauthorized record modifications, and loss of data integrity or traceability. No experimental cyberattack demonstrated.
lifecycle_stage: Digital manufacturing records, production tracking, post-processing documentation, and quality assurance.
purdue_level: L5–L4 quality/part-record web application and decentralized storage; L0 manufacturing is the source of recorded data.
threat_model: The paper motivates prevention of untraceable/unauthorized quality-record changes; a concrete attacker, capabilities and malicious trial are not established in the reviewed study.

paper: Blockchain-Based Traceability and Management for Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks, replay attacks, unauthorized transactions, transaction tampering, and intellectual property/copyright infringement. No experimental attack demonstrated.
lifecycle_stage: Order authorization, digital-design management, production tracking, and product certification.
purdue_level: L5–L4 enterprise smart-contract, design and certification records; L2–L0 workshop/sensor data are represented in the workflow.
threat_model: Design owners, workshops and customers exchange designs and records; threat analysis considers unauthorized modification and replay, assuming protected participant private keys.

paper: Characteristic Aspects of Additive Manufacturing Security From Security Awareness Perspectives
attacks_mentioned: Technical data/IP theft, spear-phishing, network session hijacking, side-channel information leakage, part sabotage, equipment damage, and unauthorized or illegal part manufacturing.
lifecycle_stage: Digital-design protection, manufacturing security, post-processing concerns, inspection, and risk management.
purdue_level: L5–L4 enterprise/data governance, L3 AM engineering, L2–L0 manufacturing and inspection, according to component discussed.
threat_model: Security-awareness analysis compares adversaries seeking technical-data theft, sabotage and illicit manufacture; attacker access and goals differ across reviewed scenarios.

paper: Comprehensive Threat Analysis in Additive Manufacturing Supply Chain: A Hybrid Qualitative and Quantitative Risk Assessment Framework
attacks_mentioned: CAD/STL manipulation, IP theft, side-channel attacks, product-property sabotage, equipment manipulation, material contamination, and unauthorized access. Also considers non-adversarial operational, environmental, and financial risks.
lifecycle_stage: Digital assets, manufacturing equipment, materials, production environment, and product integrity.
purdue_level: L5–L4 supply-chain/organizational information, L3 engineering data and L2–L0 AM systems, depending on individual risk.
threat_model: Prioritizes 22 literature-derived supply-chain threats using impact/likelihood characteristics and CVE data; threat actors and capabilities vary by risk and no single exploit is tested.

paper: Confidentiality Breach Through Acoustic Side-Channel in Cyber-Physical Additive Manufacturing Systems
attacks_mentioned: Side-channel -> Acoustic attack
lifecycle_stage: Printing
purdue_level: L0 printer acoustic emissions and physical movements revealing L1 machine-control behavior.
threat_model: Acoustic eavesdropper places a recording device near the printer, models/trains stepper-motor acoustic features and infers G-code-related motion to reconstruct design IP

paper: Cross-Domain Security of Cyber-Physical Systems: A Case Study on Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Kinetic Attack
purdue_level: L0 printer motors/acoustic emissions and physical print; L1 machine control; L3 G/M-code information being inferred. Framework's demonstration analyzes the source-to-output relation.
threat_model: Models a physical-to-cyber attacker recording acoustic emissions from a target 3D printer, with a similar printer used for model training, to infer G/M-code geometry; separately discusses kinetic attack detection. Initial access to the observation position is assumed.

paper: Cyberattacks and Cybersecurity in Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Cyberattacks targeting CAD models, STL files, G-code/toolpaths, printers, sensors, actuators, and controllers; threats affecting the digital thread and physical supply chain.
lifecycle_stage: Digital assets and authorization, build preparation, machine execution, and security monitoring.
purdue_level: L5 CAD/file access; L3 slicing/toolpaths; L1 firmware/control and L0 printer/sensors
threat_model: Narrative survey covers CAD/STL/G-code theft or manipulation, firmware compromise, side-channel leakage and malicious material changes. The attacker identity, access and capabilities vary by cited study; it does not define a single adversary.

paper: Cyber-Attack Vectors Focused on Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Examines cyberattack vectors affecting additive manufacturing. The specific attack methods could not be reliably established from the accessible publication information.
lifecycle_stage: Build preparation and printer execution are relevant attack surfaces, but the paper's exact coverage remains unverified.
purdue_level: L5 design/control workstation and discussed phishing; L3 exported G-code and slicer; L1 firmware execution; L0 extrusion and heated bed. Demo concerns L3 to L0 behavior.
threat_model: Assumes the attacker can edit exported G-code; demonstration manually changes extrusion and bed temperature on a Prusa i3 MK3S+. Phishing, compromised control PCs and network interfaces are discussed as possible routes, not demonstrated entry exploits.

paper: Cyber-Physical Attack Detection in Additive Manufacturing: An LSTM-Based Autoencoder Approach Using Reconstruction Error Analysis from Side-Channel Monitoring
attacks_mentioned: Cyber-physical attacks causing anomalous manufacturing-process behavior; specific attack manipulations could not be confirmed from the accessible publication material.
lifecycle_stage: In-situ monitoring and anomaly detection during printing.
purdue_level: L0 extruder/bed vibrations and accelerometers, L1 Arduino data acquisition, L2 processing/anomaly detection; L3 G-code changes provide context.
threat_model: Studies anomaly detection using accelerometer side-channel measurements and G-code-related process changes in a Prusa FFF setup. The paper does not specify a concrete adversary's initial access, attacker identity, or individual attack classes in sufficient detail.

paper: Cyber-Physical Security Vulnerabilities Identification and Classification in Smart Manufacturing - A Defense-in-Depth Driven Framework and Taxonomy
attacks_mentioned: Product-geometry manipulation, internal-defect insertion, process sabotage, equipment compromise, data exfiltration, sensor tampering, and attacks evading production monitoring or quality inspection.
lifecycle_stage: Digital-system security, process preparation and execution, monitoring, and inspection. Applicable to smart manufacturing broadly, not exclusively AM.
purdue_level: Conceptual general-manufacturing L5 web portal/cloud and enterprise data, L3 planning and instructions, L2 supervision/monitoring, L1–L0 process and inspection. AM is discussed through prior examples
threat_model: Illustrative MaaS case considers external actors accessing network/cloud to alter CAD or toolpaths and insiders with facility/data access stealing IP or sabotaging processes. Specific access is scenario-dependent; empirical AM examples are cited prior studies, not a new end-to-end attack.

paper: Cyber-Physical Vulnerabilities in Additive Manufacturing Systems: A Case Study Attack on the .STL File with Human Subjects
attacks_mentioned: altering .STL files
lifecycle_stage: Design -> Printing
purdue_level: L5/L3 STL design handling, L3 preparation and slicing, L1–L0 printing/part formation, and L2–L0 inspection equipment.
threat_model: Assumes an adversary can modify an STL design and insert internal voids to weaken a printed part while leaving exterior geometry unchanged. The study evaluates fabricated specimens and operator detection, not an actual cyber intrusion.

paper: Cybersecurity Challenges for Manufacturing Systems 4.0: Assessment of the Business Impact Level
attacks_mentioned: Analyzes potential external/insider breaches of manufacturing-data confidentiality, integrity and availability, including IP theft, altered design/process instructions and denial of service. These are assessed scenarios and literature examples, not newly executed cyberattacks.
lifecycle_stage: S1 design-information access; S2 build preparation, parameters and operation sequences; S3 execution telemetry and machine health; S5 workpiece inspection and corrective feedback. Coverage concerns data-risk assessment across these stages. Physical S4 postprocessing is not evaluated.
purdue_level: L5–L4 enterprise/business data and L3–L0 AM configuration, machine operation and inspection data; impact assessment spans these functions. Exact data-to-level assignments are contextual.
threat_model: Potential insider/external actors compromise manufacturing-data confidentiality, integrity or availability, causing IP theft, changes or disruption. The assessment does not define a single attack chain or required attacker access.

paper: Cybersecurity for digital manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Reviews unauthorized access, DoS, MitM, malware and data manipulation. Two AM scenarios concern unauthorized cloud-CAD geometry changes (bracket defects examined using finite-element analysis) and controller/program tampering that changes toolpath, units, temperature or feed rate; physical-access and compromised-host routes are discussed, not demonstrated as printer exploits.
lifecycle_stage: S1 design-asset access/authorization; S2 CAD-to-toolpath preparation and parameter manipulation; S3 controller access, firmware and build execution. S5 nondestructive inspection is a recommended defensive opportunity. No substantive S4 analysis identified.
purdue_level: L5 enterprise design/cloud access; L3 CAD/toolpath preparation; L1 controller and L0 printer; L2 monitoring and L0 inspection are discussed defences.
threat_model: Reviews multiple threats. Illustrative adversaries alter cloud CAD through account/host access or change controller programs via local or compromised-host access; the paper describes scenarios, not demonstrated intrusions.

paper: Cybersecurity of Industrial Cyber-Physical Systems: A Review
attacks_mentioned: Reviews industrial cyber/physical incidents and classifies sector, threat source, motivation, scope, domain, mechanism, active/passive type and affected CIA properties. Covers unauthorized access, malware and manipulation of control/sensor behavior; no AM-specific attack experiment is presented.
lifecycle_stage: AM lifecycle stage not established. This industrial-control survey is contextual evidence; possible relevance to S3 control/monitoring; not an AM application studied in the paper.
purdue_level: No AM-specific Purdue placement established. The industrial-control review is contextually relevant to monitoring and control functions; do not count as an AM-specific level assignment.
threat_model: Industrial CPS survey covering unauthorized access, malware and control/sensor manipulation across many attacker types. It does not define one AM-specific attacker or required access.

paper: Cybersecurity risks and mitigation strategies in additive manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Reviews IP theft, design/STL corruption, malicious G-code or firmware, altered build orientation, and side-channel leakage. Examples of voids and mechanically weakened parts come from cited studies rather than new attacks.
lifecycle_stage: S1 design/IP handling; S2 conversion/toolpath preparation; S3 printer/firmware operation. S4 finishing is named without a distinct safeguard. Final checking is a conceptual received-model comparison; operational S5 inspection is not demonstrated.
purdue_level: L3 design/build-file preparation; L1 firmware/control and L0 physical printer emissions. These represent reviewed functions, not a tested system architecture.
threat_model: Reviews design/STL corruption, malicious G-code or firmware, IP theft and side-channel leakage; attacker access and capabilities vary by cited scenario and no single threat model is specified.

paper: Decoding Intellectual Property: Acoustic and Magnetic Side-Channel Attack on a 3D Printer
venue: Security and Privacy in Cyber-Physical Systems and Smart Vehicles / Springer; 2025
attacks_mentioned: Demonstrates passive IP theft: a nearby smartphone records acoustic and magnetic emissions while a printer operates; trained movement classifiers reconstruct G-code without modifying the printer.
lifecycle_stage: S3: emissions are captured during build execution; reconstructed toolpaths expose design IP. S4 and S5 are not studied.
purdue_level: L0 physical printer emissions observed externally; disclosed information concerns process-control instructions at L1.
threat_model: Passive IP thief places a smartphone close to a running printer to record acoustic and magnetic emissions and infer G-code; no printer modification is required. Trained movement classifiers and nearby sensor access are assumed.

paper: Detecting cyber-physical attacks in CyberManufacturing systems with machine learning methods
attacks_mentioned: Models replacement of STL files with hidden infill voids and simulates five defect patterns. A separate CNC example modifies geometry or machining operation; it is not an AM attack experiment.
lifecycle_stage: S1–S2: malicious design substitution; S3: camera monitoring and alerts during printing. It detects introduced defects without independently proving malicious intent or implementing postprocessing security.
purdue_level: L3 model/toolpath preparation and L0 printer/camera observation; L2 supervisory alerting where used.
threat_model: Simulated attacker replaces an STL with hidden infill voids; the AM tests assume access to substitute the file, not a demonstrated network compromise. A separate CNC example must not be treated as AM.

paper: Detecting Sabotage Attacks in Additive Manufacturing Using Actuator Power Signatures
attacks_mentioned:
*  Sabotage Attack
*
lifecycle_stage: Printing
purdue_level: L3 model and job transfer, L1 actuator control and L0 actuator power; independent power monitoring supports L2 process analysis.
threat_model: Assumes model, host computer, communication network or printer can be compromised and used to sabotage a part; a trusted benign print produces a reference actuator-power signature. Initial compromise is assumed rather than the detector's demonstrated entry step.

paper: Digital Audio Signature for 3D Printing Integrity
venue: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security; 2018
attacks_mentioned:
* Sabotage Attack
* Side-channel attacks
lifecycle_stage: Printing
purdue_level: L3 STL/G-code and trusted reference handling, L1 stepper control, L0 printer acoustics, and L2 independent audio-signature comparison.
threat_model: Assumes original file/host/network/printer may be compromised to manipulate toolpath commands; a signed master acoustic fingerprint is generated from a verified benign reference print and compared against later stepper-motor audio.

paper: Digitally Twinned Additive Manufacturing: Detecting Flaws in Laser Powder Bed Fusion by Combining Thermal Simulations with In-situ Meltpool Sensor Data
attacks_mentioned: Emulates cyber sabotage by embedding internal spherical voids through selective laser suppression. Separate cases examine laser-power changes and lens delamination; these are induced flaw mechanisms, not demonstrated network intrusions.
lifecycle_stage: S2 covers thermal-model preparation; S3 is the in-process detection focus. Post-build characterization validates the method and does not by itself establish operational S5 protection; S4 is not demonstrated.
purdue_level: L3 thermal simulation, L2 in-situ monitoring, and L0 LPBF machine/meltpool; L0 physical XCT inspection supports evaluation.
threat_model: Cyber-sabotage motivation: selective suppression of laser exposure emulates internal voids. The study induces defects and does not demonstrate an attacker or access path.

paper: Digital Twin and Cybersecurity in Additive Manufacturing
venue: Journal of Cybersecurity Education, Research and Practice; 2024
attacks_mentioned: Reviews AM threats including design/process tampering, sensor and network spoofing, denial of service, malicious software, and attacks on digital-twin data or models; no new adversarial experiment is performed.
lifecycle_stage: S1 design/data governance; S2 simulation/planning; S3 process monitoring/control. Table VI also reviews S4 postprocessing and S5 quality measurement within a lifecycle DT framework. These are literature coverage, not independently evaluated security at every stage.
purdue_level: Broad review spans L5–L4 data/management, L3 engineering and L2–L0 production and inspection; individual prior examples vary in scope.
threat_model: Survey of data/model manipulation, spoofing, denial of service and theft across digital twins and AM; attacker privileges and access are case-specific and no new attacker experiment is defined.

paper: Digital Twin-Based Cyber-Attack Detection Framework for Cyber-Physical Manufacturing Systems
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering; 2024
attacks_mentioned: Simulates network attacks on a printer temperature-measurement stream using constant-offset and cyclic injections. These interfere with closed-loop heating control; fan cooling and degraded controller response serve as non-attack anomalies.
lifecycle_stage: S3: heating control, sensor-stream monitoring, and attack detection during printing. No postprocessing or product-certification mechanism is evaluated.
purdue_level: L2 monitoring/digital twin; L1 controller and L0 temperature sensor/heating physical process.
threat_model: Models injected constant-offset and cyclic attacks against a networked temperature measurement stream. Attacker can alter that signal

paper: Digital Twins, AI, and Cybersecurity in Additive Manufacturing: A Comprehensive Review of Current Trends and Challenges
attacks_mentioned: Reviews hardware, firmware, network, data, and side-channel threats to AM, including sabotage and IP disclosure. Attack examples and performance results are drawn from earlier publications.
lifecycle_stage: S1 access/IP governance; S2 toolpath and parameter simulation; S3 monitoring/adaptive control; S5 proposed final-part authorization and quality-record traceability. These are reviewed/proposed functions; S4 protection is not separately demonstrated.
purdue_level: Architecture spans L5–L4 data/access management, L3 preparation and L2–L0 monitoring and execution; placement is inferred from component functions.
threat_model: Reviews attacks on AM data, networks, firmware, hardware and side channels; cited threat models differ and the paper does not demonstrate an original attack.

paper: dr0wned: Cyber-Physical Attack with Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned:
*  Sabotage Attack
*
lifecycle_stage: Attack in Design flow
purdue_level: L5 user workstation/email and design files; L3 print preparation; L1–L0 print execution and physical propeller.
threat_model: Adversary sends a malicious archive to a printer operator, compromises the control computer, modifies a propeller STL and seeks premature failure during drone flight. Access relies on victim interaction and a vulnerable desktop workflow; tested specific printer/drone and malicious design.

paper: Dynamic-Thermal and Localized Filament-Kinetic Attacks on Fused Filament Fabrication Based 3D Printing Process
attacks_mentioned: Demonstrates localized filament-kinetic and dynamic-thermal sabotage under compromised G-code/firmware. Retraction, extrusion-state or speed changes create internal defects; nozzle-temperature changes alter material properties while limiting visible or nozzle-motion changes.
lifecycle_stage: S2: malicious build instructions; S3: extrusion and thermal manipulation during execution. Mechanical testing evaluates attack effects rather than establishing S5 operational inspection.
purdue_level: L3 G-code preparation, L1 firmware/control, and L0 extrusion and thermal physical process.
threat_model: Assumes compromised G-code or firmware enables targeted extrusion/retraction or nozzle-temperature changes to weaken internal material while minimizing visible changes. Initial compromise mechanism is not demonstrated.

paper: Embedding of Taggants in the Vat Photo-Polymerisation Additive Manufacturing Process for Anti-Counterfeiting Measures
attacks_mentioned: Targets counterfeit parts and physical copying of embedded identifiers, including an adversary possessing reference coordinates, color codes, and raw materials. Adversarial cloning is discussed rather than experimentally attempted.
lifecycle_stage: S2: layer-thickness selection; S3: resin preparation and taggant embedding; S4: washing and UV/thermal post-curing; S5: optical/XCT enrollment and proposed customer authentication.
purdue_level: L0 physical incorporation of resin/taggants and XCT/optical inspection
threat_model: Counterfeiter aims to reproduce authenticated parts and may know reference coordinates, colour codes and raw materials; cloning is discussed, not experimentally attempted.

paper: Embedding Tracking Codes in Additive Manufactured Parts for Product Authentication
attacks_mentioned: Considers economically motivated counterfeiters with genuine parts and reverse-engineering capability, as well as unauthorized reproduction enabled by stolen design files. It does not demonstrate a network intrusion.
lifecycle_stage: Reviewer mapping: S1: code-bearing design creation; S2: segmentation and build parameters; S3: embedding during manufacture; S5: nondestructive reading for authentication. S4 is a compatibility limitation because heat treatment or hot isostatic pressing can destroy codes.
purdue_level: Reviewer mapping: L3 embedded-code preparation; L0 printing, physical part and micro-CT inspection; L2 inspection workflow where applicable.
threat_model: Counterfeiter can acquire genuine parts and attempt reverse engineering, or exploit stolen design files for unauthorized reproduction; no network intrusion is demonstrated.

paper: Encryption is Futile: Reconstructing 3D-Printed Models using the Power Side-Channel
attacks_mentioned: Demonstrates IP reconstruction by a malicious AM provider or insider who can instrument individual printer actuators. Current measurements reveal motor motion and extrusion even when customer files and communication remain encrypted.
lifecycle_stage: S1: outsourced manufacturing and IP exposure; S3: actuator instrumentation and observation during printing. Reconstruction is not an S5 product-inspection defence.
purdue_level: L0 motor current and physical emissions, exposing L1 actuator-control information.
threat_model: Malicious AM provider or insider with physical access instruments individual actuator currents to reconstruct customer geometry despite encrypted files/communications.

paper: Engineering Attack Vectors and Detecting Anomalies in Additive Manufacturing
venue: Security and Privacy in Cyber-Physical Systems and Smart Vehicles, 2026
attacks_mentioned: Demonstrates host-root compromise and a rogue control interface enabling uploaded or live G-code manipulation, including extrusion changes, cavities, dimensional changes, and noise injection. Weak-password experiments use deliberately permissive lab configurations.
lifecycle_stage: S2: file and parameter manipulation before release; S3: live control interference and log monitoring during execution. No operational postprocessing or certification mechanism is evaluated.
purdue_level: L3 job/G-code preparation; L2 printer host/control interface and logs; L1 controller and L0 physical process.
threat_model: Host-root compromise and rogue interface allow attacker to upload/modify live G-code or change extrusion. Weak-password tests used deliberately permissive lab settings.

paper: Enhanced anti-counterfeiting measures for additive manufacturing: coupling lanthanide nanomaterial chemical signatures with blockchain technology
attacks_mentioned: Addresses counterfeit printed parts and fraudulent digital provenance, including the possibility of compromised manufacturer credentials.
lifecycle_stage: S1 covers recorded design/provenance information; S3 embeds taggants during printing; S5 covers post-production authenticity checks and custody verification. No finishing-stage S4 defence is shown.
purdue_level: L0 taggants/part, UV and smartphone optical verification; L5 enterprise blockchain/provenance record.
threat_model: Counterfeiters create fake printed parts or provenance and may compromise manufacturer credentials.

paper: Ensuring Additive Manufacturing Quality and Cyber–Physical Security via Side-Channel Measurements and Transmissions
attacks_mentioned: Studies malicious alterations after trusted toolpath/signature creation: internal voids, changed infill settings and line-level extrusion edits. An altered design incorporated into the original reference signature would evade this premise.
lifecycle_stage: S2 covers signature generation and toolpath encoding; S3 covers physical transmission and build monitoring. No actual S4 intervention or operational S5 certification procedure is demonstrated.
purdue_level: L3 trusted job/signature creation; L1 toolpath/control commands; L0 motion/extrusion/temperature sensing with independent monitor.
threat_model: Assumes trusted creation of baseline toolpath/signature; an attacker alters geometry, infill or extrusion commands afterwards. Corruption before signature creation is outside the detection premise.

paper: Evaluation of a Cyber-Physical Attack Effectiveness in Metal Additive Manufacturing by Selectively Modifying Build Layer Thickness
attacks_mentioned: Demonstrates metal-LPBF sabotage through build-design partitioning and zero core-laser exposure in selected internal layers while retaining contour scans. This emulates increased effective layer thickness without requiring compromised firmware.
lifecycle_stage: S1–S2: design partitioning and exposure-parameter edits; S3: targeted unfused layers; S4: heat treatment of 17-4PH specimens; S5: X-ray inspection assesses detectability.
purdue_level: L3 build preparation and laser-exposure instructions; L1 machine control; L0 LPBF and tomography inspection (CT Scan).
threat_model: Sabotage is emulated through build design partitioning and suppressed internal core-laser exposure while retaining contours; ability to modify preparation/build specifications is assumed, not achieved through network intrusion.

paper: Evaluation of Additive and Subtractive Manufacturing from the Security Perspective
attacks_mentioned: Analyzes technical-data theft, sabotage, and illegal object manufacture across additive and subtractive manufacturing. Threat paths include compromised design/control data, software or firmware, physical materials, insiders, and power supply.
lifecycle_stage: S1: designers, service relationships, and technical-data transfer; S2–S3: toolpaths, materials, and process control. S4 finishing and S5 nondestructive inspection are explicitly considered in the workflow, without validated stage-specific defences.
purdue_level: L3 engineering/design preparation and L2–L0 manufacturing execution; broad AM/subtractive comparison, not a specific deployed architecture.
threat_model: Qualitative threat analysis considers data theft, sabotage and illegal production via compromised design/control data, software/firmware, materials, insiders or power; capabilities depend on scenario.

paper: Firewall3D: A Hardware Firewall for Defending 3D Printers Against Firmware Attacks
attacks_mentioned: Considers a compromised motherboard or firmware that alters motion, extrusion, thermal control, fans, or homing to sabotage parts, damage equipment, or facilitate leakage. Attacker control of the defensive hardware is excluded.
lifecycle_stage: S3: machine homing, actuator operation, heating/cooling, and execution-time detection. Installation requires physical wiring access
purdue_level: L2 supervisory PC/security channel, L1 independent hardware firewall and printer controller, L0 actuator/sensor signals and machine process.
threat_model: Assumes malicious printer motherboard/firmware controls motion, extrusion, thermal/fan and homing behavior; defender hardware and its trusted firmware are outside attacker control.

paper: Fix the Leak! An Information Leakage Aware Secured Cyber-Physical Manufacturing System
attacks_mentioned: Side-channel attacks
lifecycle_stage: Slicing -> Printing
purdue_level: L3 CAM/toolpath generation, L1 control outputs, L0 printer emissions. Mapping indicates leakage and mitigation locations
threat_model: Attacker observes acoustic, power or electromagnetic emissions from a running AM machine to infer G-code or design information; practical sensing access and physical positioning vary by scenario. The defense adjusts CAM-generated instructions.

paper: FLAW3D: A Trojan-Based Cyber Attack on the Physical Outcomes of Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned:
* Trojan Attack 1: Material Reduction
* Trojan Attack 2: Material Relocation
lifecycle_stage: OS -> Printing
purdue_level: L1 bootloader, firmware and command interception; L0 printer actuation and resulting part. L3 build instructions are manipulated during execution.
threat_model: Attacker can install a malicious bootloader on an AVR-based Marlin-compatible printer; Trojan hides from verification tools and changes execution to weaken printed parts. Initial installation access is assumed.

paper: Forensics of Thermal Side-Channel in Additive Manufacturing Systems
attacks_mentioned: Investigates thermal side-channel IP leakage by recording a printer from within 95 cm and inferring nozzle/bed motion. The attack requires a camera view and prior knowledge of printer kinematics.
lifecycle_stage: S3: thermal observation of build execution. The analysis reconstructs manufacturing information; it does not provide operational S5 authentication or forensics deployment.
purdue_level: L0 thermal emissions and physical nozzle/bed motion, revealing aspects of L1 motion commands.
threat_model: Adversary records printer thermal emissions from a camera viewpoint within tested proximity and uses prior printer kinematics to infer motion and steal design information.

paper: FRoMEPP: Digital Forensic Readiness Framework for Material Extrusion Based 3D Printing Process
attacks_mentioned: Assumes a knowledgeable adversary can compromise cyber components or firmware to sabotage extrusion printing. Demonstrated cases involve internal cavities, localized thermal changes, and timing manipulation; passive side-channel IP theft is excluded.
lifecycle_stage: S1–S2: design, application, and build-file artifacts; S3: independent process monitoring and printer records; S5: post-incident investigation and feedback from failed parts. No S4 finishing security is demonstrated.
purdue_level: L2 forensic collection/logging, L1 firmware/controller and L0 extrusion and independent sensors; security correlation can include L3 job data.
threat_model: Assumes knowledgeable attacker compromises a cyber component or firmware to introduce cavities, thermal alterations or timing sabotage; passive side-channel IP theft is outside scope.

paper: Hiding My Real Self! Protecting Intellectual Property in 3D Printing Systems
attacks_mentioned: OPTICAL SIDE-CHANNEL ATTACK
lifecycle_stage: Printing
purdue_level: L0 printer movements and projected optical signals; L2 camera acquisition/monitoring; L3 inferred toolpath is the protected information asset.
threat_model: Attacker obtains camera video of a 3D printer and uses learned image analysis to infer printhead trajectory/design. Defense analysis considers a stronger adversary aware of projected noise who trains on noisy images.

paper: How to Ensure Bad Quality in Metal Additive Manufacturing: In-Situ Infrared Thermography from the Security Perspective
attacks_mentioned: Assumes an adversary can manipulate IR thermography components or feedback. Analyzes calibration, camera, reference-data, shutter and control-loop tampering, which can distort laser control or mislead quality decisions; initial compromise is outside scope.
lifecycle_stage: S3 covers compromised sensing and closed-loop processing. S5 quality decisions are analyzed for open-loop thermography, but not experimentally attacked in a qualification workflow. S4 consequences are discussed, without demonstrated intervention.
purdue_level: L2 thermography/quality monitoring, L1 feedback control and L0 IR sensors and laser process.
threat_model: Assumes attacker access to IR thermography/feedback components can tamper with calibration, camera, reference data, shutter or control loops to affect quality and control; initial compromise unspecified.

paper: Identifying 3D printer residual data via open-source documentation
attacks_mentioned: Identifies potential leakage of residual design/G-code data and tampering opportunities along removable-media and network transfer paths. These are inferred risks rather than newly executed attacks.
lifecycle_stage: S2 covers slicing-host files and command transfer; S3 covers printer execution/storage. Incident forensics and privacy analysis are not equivalent to S5 product inspection; S4 is not established.
purdue_level: L3 build host and removable/job media; L2 printer interfaces/network transfer and L1 controller storage depending on device. Exact placement is model-dependent.
threat_model: Considers residual-file disclosure and data tampering on printer media or network transfers. The paper infers possible access surfaces from documentation rather than demonstrating acquisition or attacks.

paper: Identifying Cyber-Physical Vulnerabilities in Additive Manufacturing Systems using a Systems Approach
venue: 2020 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC); 2020
attacks_mentioned: Analyzes technical-data theft through compromised networks/equipment, insiders, communication interception, side channels and equipment analysis. The case study selects these threats from prior literature rather than executing new attacks.
lifecycle_stage: S1 covers technical-data access and architectural security decisions; S3 includes exposure through manufacturing emissions. The analysis spans infrastructure conceptually, without demonstrating stage-specific S2, S4 or S5 protection.
purdue_level: L5–L4 enterprise/communications context, L3 engineering information, L2–L1 printer/control interfaces and L0 acoustic emissions, depending on scenario.
threat_model: Works through technical-data theft from communications, equipment, insiders and side channels using prior literature; no one access path or new intrusion demonstrated.

paper: Identifying the Cyber-Incidents in Additive Manufacturing Systems via Multimedia Signals
venue: ASME International Symposium on Flexible Automation (ISFA 2020); 2020
attacks_mentioned: Mimics sabotage by changing a cube’s internal infill from 100% to 50%, while considering broader upstream compromises that ultimately alter extruder motion. No initial cyber intrusion is implemented.
lifecycle_stage: S3 covers in-process audio/video monitoring; S2 G-code supplies an optional trusted comparison. No operational S4 intervention or S5 certification is demonstrated.
purdue_level: L3 trusted G-code/reference, L2 monitoring, L1 motion commands and L0 extruder audio/video emissions.
threat_model: Emulates sabotage by changing cube infill from 100% to 50%; assumes a resulting modified print trajectory. Initial attacker access and cyber intrusion are not established.

paper: Implementing the Risk Management Framework for Additive Manufacturing Security: A Model-Based Approach
attacks_mentioned: Analyzes technological risks to LPBF product quality and intellectual property. An altered build file and scan strategy illustrate a threat/failure path; the paper does not execute an intrusion or sabotage attack.
lifecycle_stage: S1: mission, assets, stakeholders, authorization and requirements; S2: build-file verification and preparation; S3: modeled machine, powder, and sensing flows. S4–S5 security controls are not independently validated.
purdue_level: L3 build file and scan-strategy engineering, L2 supervisory information flows and L1–L0 LPBF operation. Model-based RMF planning spans system boundaries.
threat_model: Examines LPBF technological risks including a modified build file and scan strategy affecting quality/IP; attacker privileges and intrusion route are not demonstrated.

paper: Implications of Malicious 3D Printer Firmware
attacks_mentioned: Installs modified Marlin firmware on a Printrbot and triggers malicious behavior with a fan command. One version substitutes a pyramid for a requested cube; another increases extrusion while leaving incoming command validation intact.
lifecycle_stage: S3 is the core stage: firmware interprets commands and controls deposition. Printed-output inspection evaluates effects rather than establishing an operational S5 defence; S4 is not covered.
purdue_level: L1 printer firmware/controller and L0 extruder/printer process; L2 host acknowledgments/logs.
threat_model: Assumes ability to install malicious printer firmware; hidden behavior is triggered by a fan command, substituting geometry or increasing extrusion while retaining normal logging in the latter case.

paper: Information Leakage-Aware Computer-Aided Cyber-Physical Manufacturing
venue: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security; 2018
attacks_mentioned: Side-channel attacks
lifecycle_stage: Slicing -> Printing
purdue_level: L3 CAM slicing/toolpath/orientation selection, L1 machine control, and L0 acoustic/power/magnetic/vibration emissions from the physical FDM printer.
threat_model: Assumes adversary has unlimited access to a replica printer for supervised leakage-model training and can observe physical side-channel emissions to infer G/M-code; leakage-aware CAM changes orientation and speed to reduce information exposure.

paper: Intellectual Property Protection in Additive Layer Manufacturing: Requirements for Secure Outsourcing
venue: Proceedings of the 4th Program Protection and Reverse Engineering Workshop; 2014
attacks_mentioned: Considers malicious designers, process-tuning experts, manufacturers and external adversaries stealing geometry/process IP, bypassing production licenses, intercepting transfers or reverse engineering parts and emissions.
lifecycle_stage: S1 covers licensing and cross-party access; S2 covers process-parameter specification; S3 covers protected execution and side-channel risks. Attribution of manufactured objects is a proposed downstream function, not a demonstrated S5 inspection workflow; S4 is not established.
purdue_level: L5–L4 outsourcing/authorization, L3 engineering/process data, and L0 physical parts/emissions; reviewed access paths do not imply an implemented architecture.
threat_model: Considers dishonest designers, tuning experts, manufacturers and outsiders seeking geometry/process IP or unlicensed production via transfer interception, reverse engineering and physical emissions; capabilities vary by role.

paper: KCAD: Kinetic Cyber-Attack Detection Method for Cyber-Physical Additive Manufacturing Systems
attacks_mentioned: Kinetic Attack
lifecycle_stage: Printing
purdue_level: L5 CAD/design and L3 slicing/instructions, L1 printer firmware/control and L0 acoustic emissions/physical motions; L2 independent KCAD analysis.
threat_model: Attacker can alter CAD, slicing or firmware information flow, changing machine control parameters to create physical defects. Evaluation implements firmware changes to motion speed, axis and distance; initial compromise is assumed.

paper: Layered Security Guidance for Data Asset Management in Additive Manufacturing
venue: Journal of Computing and Information Science in Engineering, 24(7); 2024
attacks_mentioned: Reviews AM data theft, sabotage, and unauthorized manufacture to motivate risk-based guidance. Design-to-toolpath conversions and data relationships create opportunities for malicious geometry or parameter changes; no new attack is executed.
lifecycle_stage: S1: governance, responsibilities, and data assets; S2: geometry/process definitions and format conversion; S3: machine/process data relationships. Postproduction is contextual, with no distinct S4 or S5 intervention demonstrated.
purdue_level: L5–L4 data management and governance, L3 engineering assets and L2–L0 production data assets; layered guidance spans rather than validates a specific deployment.
threat_model: AM guidance considers data theft, sabotage and unauthorized manufacture. Data conversion and dependencies create manipulation opportunities; no single attacker or new attack is implemented.

paper: Leave Your Phone at the Door: Side Channels that Reveal Factory Floor Secrets
venue: Proceedings of the 2016 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security; 2016
attacks_mentioned: Demonstrates phone-based acoustic and magnetic leakage from a 3D printer and CNC mill, allowing reconstruction of manufacturing outlines. A reference-signature library, knowledge of operating conditions, domain constraints, and human assistance support inference.
lifecycle_stage: S3: emissions are recorded during manufacturing and converted into design/process information.
purdue_level: L0 physical machine emissions revealing L1 movement/control behavior; phone is external observer.
threat_model: Phone-equipped adversary gathers acoustic/magnetic emissions near a 3D printer or CNC mill, aided by calibrated reference signatures, operating knowledge and human segmentation, to infer outlines.

paper: Leveraging Memory Forensics to Investigate and Detect Illegal 3D Printing Activities
attacks_mentioned: Demonstrates a local-root attacker modifying G-code during Cura/CuraEngine inter-process communication, including thermal, cooling, and layer-height changes. Illegal-printing investigations motivate artifact recovery, but suspicious files alone do not establish intent.
lifecycle_stage: S2: slicing-memory acquisition and manipulation detection; S3: downstream printing effects.
purdue_level: L3 slicer host, in-memory geometry, settings and G-code; evaluated manipulation happens before physical execution.
threat_model: Adversary with local root access changes G-code in Cura/CuraEngine inter-process communication; forensic investigators recover volatile artifacts to detect inconsistent settings and support investigation.

paper: Low-Magnitude Infill Structure Manipulation Attacks on Fused Filament Fabrication 3D Printers
attacks_mentioned: An insider intercepts an unencrypted printer connection using ARP poisoning and alters G-code coordinates. Two attacks increase infill-line or vertex spacing to create internal weak regions while compensating motion/material totals. Low-magnitude changes target the tolerance of monitoring schemes.
lifecycle_stage: S2 covers G-code integrity before execution; S3 covers altered internal deposition; S5 covers evaluated micro-CT inspection. No operational S4 intervention is established.
purdue_level: L2 host/printer communications, L1 controller commands and L0 printed infill and micro-CT inspection; source G-code originates at L3.
threat_model: Insider with access to an unencrypted printer connection uses ARP poisoning to intercept and alter G-code coordinates, subtly weakening infill while controlling aggregate motion/material changes.

paper: Machine Learning-Based Early Detection of Malicious G-code Manipulations in 3D Printing
attacks_mentioned: Studies malicious filament-flow, thermal-control and Z-profile changes embedded in G-code, including cavities, extrusion-state changes, fan or temperature changes, and layer-height manipulation.
lifecycle_stage: S2 is the defensive focus through preprint instruction analysis; S3 appears in physical attack demonstrations. S4 and operational S5 coverage are not established.
purdue_level: L3 build-file preparation and G-code screening; L1 commands and L0 physical print case studies.
threat_model: Adversary modifies preprint G-code to manipulate flow, temperature, fan or layer height. The evaluation studies generated attack files rather than establishing an initial compromise route.

paper: Machine Learning-Based Investigation of the 3D Printer Cooling Effect on Print Quality in Fused Filament Fabrication: A Cybersecurity Perspective
attacks_mentioned: Assumes a remote adversary can change cooling-fan settings during fused-filament fabrication, potentially degrading the surface quality of a printed part.
lifecycle_stage: S2 covers parameter/model preparation; S3 covers checking cooling commands during printing. Roughness measurements support development and evaluation, without establishing an operational S5 inspection defence.
purdue_level: L2 OctoPrint host/plugin, L1 fan commands and L0 printer/fan and surface inspection.
threat_model: Assumes a remote adversary can manipulate cooling-fan settings, affecting print surface quality. The work does not demonstrate the initial network exploit.

paper: Manipulation of G-code Toolpath Files in 3D Printers
attacks_mentioned: With root access to a local slicing host, an attacker scans the running slicer’s heap, reconstructs ASCII G-code fragments and overwrites equal-length bytes. Demonstrated changes lower selected-layer temperature or omit infill while preserving plausible toolpath files.
lifecycle_stage: S2 is the compromise point inside the slicer; S3 executes the malicious thermal and deposition instructions. Mechanical tests evaluate consequences and do not alone establish S5 coverage; S4 is not demonstrated.
purdue_level: L3 slicer host and in-memory G-code; L1 controller instructions and L0 printed specimen effects.
threat_model: Attacker with local root access scans a slicer heap and overwrites readable ASCII G-code fragments using equal-length substitutions to change temperature or omit infill.

paper: Manufacturing and Security Challenges in 3D Printing
attacks_mentioned: Malicious and deliberate modification of the print orientation
lifecycle_stage: Design -> Slicing -> Printing
purdue_level: L3 build orientation/design inputs, L1–L0 fabrication and L2–L0 ultrasonic/material inspection. Attribution of edits to a real cyber intrusion is not established.
threat_model: Considers malicious alteration of print orientation or embedded defects that can weaken a part; experiments assess modified specimens. Specific attacker identity and digital entry route are not demonstrated.

paper: Materials vs digits: A review of embedded anti-counterfeiting fingerprints in three-dimensional printing
venue: Materials Science and Engineering: R: Reports; 2024
attacks_mentioned: Reviews counterfeiting and unauthorized reproduction enabled by stolen designs, copied material formulations or reverse engineering of printed objects. It introduces no new cyberattack experiment.
lifecycle_stage: S1–S2 include designing/encoding authentication features; S3 embeds or generates them; S5 verifies provenance/authenticity. S4 finishing and heat treatment are discussed as feature-survival constraints, without a newly evaluated postprocessing defence.
purdue_level: L3 digital watermark/model creation and L0 physical taggants, printed-part authentication and measurement; exact components vary across studies.
threat_model: Surveys counterfeiting via stolen designs, copied material formulations and reverse engineering of parts. Individual attacks and required access vary across cited literature; no original adversarial trial.

paper: MitM Attacks on Intellectual Property and Integrity of Additive Manufacturing Systems: A Security Analysis
attacks_mentioned: Demonstrates LAN man-in-the-middle attacks on a Stratasys Dimension Elite: stealing transmitted proprietary CMB models, substituting another model and replacing internal part material with support material. ARP poisoning and a protocol-aware proxy enable interception.
lifecycle_stage: S2 covers transfer and integrity of prepared toolpaths; S3 realizes material substitutions during fabrication. Compression testing evaluates consequences rather than constituting an operational S5 defence;
purdue_level: L2 networked host/printer interface, L1 machine/control job execution and L0 resulting physical part; L3 design file is affected.
threat_model: LAN attacker uses ARP poisoning and a protocol-aware proxy to intercept a Stratasys workflow, steal CMB models, substitute jobs or replace internal build material.

paper: Model-Based Security Analysis in Additive Manufacturing Systems
venue: ACM CCS Workshop on Additive Manufacturing Security (AMSec@CCS); 2022
attacks_mentioned: Models potential confidentiality, integrity and availability failures in a representative modified laser-AM architecture, including vulnerable I/O and controller paths.
lifecycle_stage: Modeled assets span S2 part-description transfer and S3 controller/laser operation; analysis occurs before deployment. No operational S4 or S5 workflow is evaluated.
purdue_level: L3 engineering/security modeling, L2 supervisory interfaces, L1 modeled controllers and L0 physical process. Assignments are functional model interpretations.
threat_model: Models potential CIA violations through modeled I/O and controller vulnerabilities in a representative laser-AM architecture

paper: Modeling of smart additive manufacturing processes for attack analysis and detection
venue: 2025 33rd Euromicro International Conference on Parallel, Distributed, and Network-Based Processing (PDP); 2025
attacks_mentioned: Simulates USB-path model theft and instruction tampering in a PC-controlled printer workflow. The altered model removes internal layer content while retaining outer contours; initial network compromise is not experimentally established.
lifecycle_stage: S2 covers prepared instructions and transfer integrity; S3 covers printer communication and execution observations. No S4 intervention or operational S5 part-certification process is established.
purdue_level: L3 PC/job preparation and recovered G-code, L2 host-to-printer communications, L1 printer control and L0 printed geometry.
threat_model: Simulates a USB-path adversary who can intercept printer traffic and steal models or tamper with instructions. Initial PC/network compromise is not established.

paper: Multi-Modal Attack Detection for Cyber-Physical Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Considers compromised firmware that changes printer actions while the reference G-code remains trusted and unmodified. Corruption upstream of that trusted reference is outside this detection premise.
lifecycle_stage: S3 covers sensing build execution and detecting firmware-induced control deviations.
purdue_level: L3 trusted G-code reference; L1 printer firmware/control; L0 acoustic, magnetic, vibration and current signals; L2 monitoring analysis.
threat_model: Assumes compromised printer firmware alters actuator behavior while original G-code is trusted. An attacker who modifies the reference before comparison is outside this premise.

paper: My Smartphone Knows What You Print: Exploring Smartphone-Based Side-Channel Attacks Against 3D Printers
attacks_mentioned: * MAGNETIC-ENHANCED IP SIDE_x0002_CHANNEL ATTACK
lifecycle_stage: Printing
purdue_level: L0 printer stepper movements and acoustic/magnetic emissions; L1 actuation creates signals; L3 reconstructed G-code is the protected asset.
threat_model: An adversary places or controls a nearby smartphone and records its acoustic and magnetic sensors to infer printer movement and reconstruct G-code or printed shapes; digital access to model files is unnecessary.

paper: Needle in a Haystack: Detecting Subtle Malicious Edits to Additive Manufacturing G-code Files
attacks_mentioned: G-Code manipulation
lifecycle_stage: G-code
purdue_level: L3 G-code preparation and offline detection, L1–L0 targeted printer execution/part consequences. The red-team exercise does not establish a network entry path.
threat_model: Red team can edit selected pre-print G-code files to introduce subtle defects; blue team must detect compromised files without knowing which are malicious or relying on a golden original model.

paper: Never Trust the Manufacturer, Never Trust the Client: A Novel Method for Streaming STL Files for Secure Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Addresses design theft and unauthorized reproduction by a manufacturer, alongside potentially harmful G-code supplied by a client. These are motivating threats; the prototype evaluation does not demonstrate a comprehensive adversarial security test.
lifecycle_stage: S1 covers controlled design disclosure; S2 covers section generation and local slicing; S3 covers streamed execution. Tensile experiments do not establish operational S5 coverage, and S4 is not demonstrated.
purdue_level: L5 client/manufacturer transfer, L3 STL sectioning/local slicing and L1–L0 printer control/execution.
threat_model: Considers a potentially dishonest manufacturer seeking the full client design and a client supplying harmful G-code. Protection assumes secure printer connection and protected memory, while manufacturer may retain slices.

paper: Obfuscation of Embedded Codes in Additive Manufactured Components for Product Authentication
attacks_mentioned: Addresses unauthorized reproduction from stolen design files or reverse-engineered parts. Counterfeiter effort is discussed, but an adversarial reverse-engineering trial is not performed.
lifecycle_stage: S1 covers protected code design; S2 controls slicing/orientation; S3 produces the embedded features; S5 reads them for authentication. The authors explicitly leave S4 postprocessing effects unstudied.
purdue_level: L3 CAD code embedding and slicing/orientation; L0 polymer printing, optical/micro-CT inspection and physical part.
threat_model: Counterfeiter may obtain design files or reverse-engineer physical parts to reproduce authenticators; paper does not experimentally attack the authentication scheme.

paper: Offensive and Defensive Perspectives in Additive Manufacturing Security
attacks_mentioned: Reviews AM threats including intellectual-property theft through files or side channels, geometry/parameter/firmware sabotage, and illegal part manufacture. Prior attacks are organized using STRIDE and by adversary intent, rather than introduced as new experiments.
lifecycle_stage: S1 includes design access and IP protection; S2 includes file and preparation integrity; S3 includes firmware, process manipulation and emissions.
purdue_level: L5 enterprise design/file access; L3 preparation files; L1–L0 printer firmware, process and emissions. Conceptual survey;
threat_model: Survey of prior threats including IP theft and sabotage; STRIDE organizes threats, rather than specifying a single attacker. Access and capabilities differ by cited study; no unified operational adversary is specified.

paper: Offramps: An FPGA-Based Intermediary for Analysis and Modification of Additive Manufacturing Control Systems
venue: 2024 54th Annual IEEE/IFIP International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks (DSN); 2024
attacks_mentioned: Demonstrates hardware interposition that changes motor, extrusion, heater, and fan control signals, enabling part alteration, denial of service, or equipment damage. Separately emulates firmware-style extrusion reduction and material relocation through modified G-code.
lifecycle_stage: S3: machine control, attack injection, and in-process monitoring. Trusted G-code/reference preparation supports S2; no actual finishing or certification workflow is evaluated.
purdue_level: L1 local controller/STEP-DIR signals and L0 actuators/physical print; L2 measurement/reference monitoring. L3 trusted G-code provides reference context.
threat_model: Adversary can physically interpose programmable hardware between controller and RAMPS and modify motor/heater/fan signals; aims include part sabotage, denial of service or equipment damage. Detector assumes a trusted reference and host link.

paper: On Cyber Sabotage Risks in Automated Manufacturing of Advanced Composites
attacks_mentioned: Analyzes sabotage of automated fibre placement through altered geometry, ply trajectories, process parameters and autoclave recipes. A phishing/USB-propagation narrative illustrates a possible attack chain and is explicitly fictional, not an executed intrusion.
lifecycle_stage: S1 includes design access; S2 includes layup planning/simulation; S3 includes robot execution and sensing; S4 explicitly includes post-layup autoclave curing. S5 nondestructive inspection appears as a future defensive direction.
purdue_level: L5 design access; L3 layup planning and simulation; L1–L0 robotic layup and autoclave operation; L2 supervision/monitoring. These are analysis targets, not observed compromise.
threat_model: Conceptual outsider/insider scenarios assume varying digital access to geometry, layup plans and process settings, or physical access for some manipulations, seeking defective composite parts. Phishing/USB infection is fictional; no live intrusion demonstrated.

paper: One Video to Steal Them All: 3D-Printing IP Theft through Optical Side-Channels
attacks_mentioned: An adversary obtains a monitoring-camera recording and reconstructs printable G-code without knowing the target instructions or object placement. The assumed video shows the whole printer; camera compromise is an entry assumption, not a demonstrated exploit.
lifecycle_stage: S3: optical leakage during printing and reconstruction from monitoring footage; the stolen G-code also exposes S2 manufacturing instructions.
purdue_level: L0 printer movements observed optically; L2 camera monitoring and video; L3 manufacturing instructions are inferred targets. Mapping describes observation and exposed asset, not demonstrated network entry.
threat_model: Attacker obtains video of a whole operating printer through a monitoring camera and seeks G-code/design reconstruction. No target instructions or object-position knowledge assumed; camera compromise is assumed, not demonstrated.

paper: Online Detection of Cyber-Incidents in Additive Manufacturing Systems via Analyzing Multimedia Signals
attacks_mentioned: Mimics sabotage by reducing internal infill while preserving the external shape of an FDM cube. The experiment changes printing conditions directly rather than demonstrating an intrusion; additional attack signals and smaller infill changes are simulated.
lifecycle_stage: S3: in-process acoustic and visual monitoring. S2 G-code supplies a trusted reference;
purdue_level: L0 printing emissions and movements; L2 camera/audio monitoring; L3 trusted G-code reference
threat_model: Hypothetical sabotage changes infill while preserving external geometry; experiments directly print altered conditions, not an intrusion. Detection assumes a trusted benign audio trace or trusted G-code; attacker access route and capabilities are not demonstrated.

paper: Operational Resilience of Additively Manufactured Parts to Stealthy Cyberphysical Attacks Using Geometric and Process Digital Twins
attacks_mentioned: Emulates stealthy attacks by removing geometric features and changing printing parameters or filament material. These introduce geometric errors, inter-line voids or overprinting; network infiltration is outside the experiments.
lifecycle_stage: S1–S2: verification and recovery of digital geometry before fabrication. S3: sensing and adaptive process correction during printing
purdue_level: L3 geometry verification/recovery and process preparation; L2 in-process sensing and adaptive supervisory response; L1–L0 motion/process control and physical printing.
threat_model: Threats include malicious geometry changes or process/material changes intended to introduce defects. Experiments emulate disturbances without demonstrating network entry; recovery relies on trusted customer reference fields and assumed secure execution.

paper: Power Consumption-Based Detection of Sabotage Attacks in Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned:
*  Sabotage Attack
*
lifecycle_stage: Printing
purdue_level: L1 actuator control and L0 actuator power; L2 independent current monitoring. Build instruction reference context is L3 when present.
threat_model: Attacker can manipulate a printer process to sabotage part quality; detector monitors current supplied to actuators and compares against a provably benign reference process.

paper: Practitioner Paper: Decoding Intellectual Property: Acoustic and Magnetic Side-channel Attack on a 3D Printer
attacks_mentioned: A nearby smartphone records acoustic and magnetic emissions from stepper-driven printing. Supervised models infer nozzle movements and reconstruct G-code, threatening design confidentiality without touching or modifying the printer.
lifecycle_stage: S3: passive observation of the active printer; recovered instructions expose S2 toolpaths. S1 outsourcing/IP access provides context, with no implemented authorization mechanism or S4/S5 intervention.
purdue_level: L0 stepper motors and physical emissions; L1 motor-control-driven motion; L3 reconstructed manufacturing instructions as the targeted information asset.
threat_model: Nearby adversary records printer acoustic and magnetic emissions using a smartphone, then applies trained models to infer motion and reconstruct toolpath/design; no physical modification or access to print files is required.

paper: Protecting Additive Manufacturing Information When Encryption Is Insufficient
venue: ASTM STP 1644: Progress in Additive Manufacturing 2021; 2022
attacks_mentioned: Analyzes an outsourced-AM scenario in which an insider obtains proprietary geometry through a printer power side channel despite encryption at rest and in transit. The technical attack is drawn from prior research, not newly demonstrated.
lifecycle_stage: S1: supplier selection, authorization, contracting, and risk planning; S3: provider-site access controls address printing emissions.
purdue_level: L5 supplier contracting and enterprise data protection; L0 printer power/physical emissions in provider facility. L3 design or instruction files are the protected information, not an evaluated compromise.
threat_model: Outsourced production scenario considers a provider insider who observes printer power and infers proprietary geometry despite encryption in storage and transit. Trust in the service provider and physical access are central assumptions; attack drawn from prior research.

paper: QuietPrint: Protecting 3D Printers Against Acoustic Side-Channel Attacks
venue: Proceedings of the 12th ACM Cyber-Physical System Security Workshop; 2026
attacks_mentioned: Studies acoustic reconstruction by a recording device near an FDM printer, using motor direction-change spikes and cooling-fan sound to infer movement. The demonstrated reconstruction uses controlled toolpaths and known motion assumptions.
lifecycle_stage: S2: modifies prepared G-code; S3: executes additional movements to obscure printing emissions.
purdue_level: L3 G-code rewriting to add decoy travel; L1–L0 motor control and motion emissions during printing. The mapping indicates defense implementation and leakage locations.
threat_model: An adversary positions an audio recorder near an FDM printer and infers movement from motor and cooling-fan sounds to reconstruct geometry. Analysis uses controlled toolpaths and stated motion assumptions.

paper: Real-time Process Authentication for Additive Manufacturing Processes based on In-situ Video Analysis
attacks_mentioned: Represents sabotage through altered internal geometry and infill orientation in FFF parts. These modifications are deliberately fabricated for detector evaluation; no network or firmware compromise is implemented.
lifecycle_stage: S3: layer-wise authentication during printing, responding to S2 geometry or toolpath alterations.
purdue_level: L0 printing and microscope observations; L2 image capture and in-process monitoring; L3 reference build configuration.
threat_model: Detection study emulates sabotage by fabricating parts with altered geometry or infill; compromise method and attacker access are not demonstrated. A trusted nominal print/reference baseline is assumed.

paper: Review, Meta-Taxonomy, and Use Cases of Cyberattack Taxonomies of Manufacturing Cybersecurity Threat Attributes and Countermeasures
attacks_mentioned: Reviews manufacturing attacks by method, target/location, and consequence, covering sabotage, information theft, and attacks on digital and physical production assets. These are synthesized prior threats, not newly executed attacks.
lifecycle_stage: Broad manufacturing review with AM design-file, build-instruction and production side-channel examples relevant to S1–S3.
purdue_level: General manufacturing taxonomy with examples involving enterprise design, engineering instructions and process/control functions; potential relevance across levels. No AM-specific deployment or precise assignment at every level established.
threat_model: Manufacturing-security taxonomy survey covers sabotage and IP theft with varied attacker access and objectives from prior works

paper: Sabotage Attack Detection for Additive Manufacturing Systems
attacks_mentioned:
*  Sabotage Attack
*
lifecycle_stage: Printing
purdue_level: L5 CAD/workstation, L3 G-code/CAM processing, L1 firmware/control parameters, L0 analog sensor emissions, and L2 multimodal inference/detection.
threat_model: Models adversaries modifying CAD/CAM software, control computers or printer firmware to alter object information and sabotage parts; illustrative infection routes are prior incidents, not newly demonstrated intrusions. Detection relies on independent side-channel sensing and original G-code-derived controls.

paper: Sabotaging Material Extrusion-Based 3D Printed Parts Through Low-Magnitude Kinetic Manipulation Attacks
