attacks_mentioned: Demonstrates network man-in-the-middle modification of G-code to weaken infill-line, infill-vertex, infill-to-wall, or interlayer bonding through small kinetic deviations. Attacks target mechanical properties while keeping external dimensions and mass apparently normal.
lifecycle_stage: S2/S3: tampered instructions and physical build execution. S5 appears in exploratory post-build micro-CT detection; destructive strength testing primarily validates attack impact.
purdue_level: L3 build instructions and transfer; L1 controller interprets modified instructions; L0 printer motions and part bonding. L2 Sophos monitoring and L0/2 micro-CT inspection are evaluated defenses.
threat_model: Network man-in-the-middle adversary can modify G-code in transit and subtly alter infill/interlayer bonding, seeking strength degradation without obvious dimensional or mass changes. The tested monitor's trust assumptions bound its evasion assessment.

paper: Sabotaging Metal Additive Manufacturing: Powder Delivery System Manipulation and Material-Dependent Effects
attacks_mentioned: Assumes an already-compromised powder-bed-fusion machine and analyzes powder-delivery manipulations that create layer, thermal, timing, or kinetic defects. Experiments simulate a selected layer-thickness attack through modified build specifications, rather than demonstrating initial machine compromise.
lifecycle_stage: S2/S3: altered build specifications and powder-layer execution; S5: inspection-evasion evaluation.
purdue_level: L3 modified build specifications; L1–L0 powder-layer actuation and metal fabrication; L2–L0 inspection instruments and analysis. Compromise path to controller is assumed, not demonstrated.
threat_model: Assumes a powder-bed-fusion machine is already compromised; attacker modifies powder delivery or effective layer thickness to create defects and degrade fatigue performance. The experiment modifies build specifications; initial access is not demonstrated.

paper: SCREAM: Secure Channels for Real-time Evaluation of Additive Manufacturing
venue: Proceedings of the 21st ACM Asia Conference on Computer and Communications Security (ASIA CCS); 2026
attacks_mentioned: Assumes attackers can alter host software, transmitted G-code, firmware or bootloader while the defender retains a trusted STL. Evaluations reproduce material reduction, relocation and internal-hole effects, without demonstrating every original compromise mechanism.
lifecycle_stage: S3: runtime actuation monitoring. S1 trusted design and S2 instructions provide references; finishing and finished-part certification are not tested.
purdue_level: L3 trusted model and instructions; L1 STEP/DIR controller signals; L0 actuators; L2 external reconstruction/monitoring. Pulse evidence is not direct measurement of deposited material.
threat_model: Attacker may modify host, G-code, firmware or bootloader to alter print geometry or material; defender has trusted STL and can physically tap motor signals. Some attacks are recreated through modified G-code, not deployed firmware malware.

paper: SECUREAM: Advancing Cybersecurity in IoT-Enabled Additive Manufacturing
venue: 2025 12th International Conference on Internet of Things: Systems, Management and Security (IOTSMS); 2025
attacks_mentioned: Identifies IP theft, data manipulation, production disruption and sabotage as risks in interconnected AM supply chains. This project description presents no executed attack or measured adversarial case.
lifecycle_stage: S1–S3 scope spans design-data sharing and manufacturing workflows.
purdue_level: L5 collaboration and authorization, L3 design/build data sharing, L2–L0 manufacturing context
threat_model: Prospective project discusses IP theft, manipulation, disruption and sabotage across connected AM supply chains. A complete attacker access/capability model and demonstrated intrusion are not reported.

paper: Securing Additive Manufacturing with Blockchain-Based Cryptographic Anchoring and Dual-Lock Integrity Auditing
attacks_mentioned: Models counterfeit products and theft or alteration of outsourced G-code by untrusted storage nodes or coordinators. Keys, management services and the permissioned blockchain trust assumptions bound the adversary; infrastructure compromise is insufficiently evaluated.
lifecycle_stage: S1 authorization and provenance, S2 stored G-code integrity, and proposed S5 product-authenticity verification.
purdue_level: L5 identity/access and shared provenance services; L3 off-chain G-code storage and integrity auditing; L2–L0 product-authentication context.
threat_model: Models untrusted storage nodes/coordinators capable of stealing or changing outsourced G-code and counterfeit production. Assumes keys and management services remain trusted and permissioned blockchain assumptions hold; attack robustness against compromised infrastructure is not established.

paper: Securing Cyber-Physical Additive Manufacturing Systems by In-Situ Process Authentication Using Streamline Video Analysis
attacks_mentioned: Simulates sabotage by rotating infill orientation or introducing an unwanted hollow feature through altered STL/slicing inputs. These changes affect printing paths; the experiment does not demonstrate initial cyber intrusion.
lifecycle_stage: S2: modeled design/slicing alterations; S3: camera acquisition and online layer authentication.
purdue_level: L3 design/slicing inputs and baseline; L2 video acquisition/statistical anomaly analysis; L0 nozzle-mounted microscope and physical print.
threat_model: Sabotage is emulated through altered STL/slicing inputs producing rotated infill or unwanted hollow features. Initial compromise route, attacker identity and access are not demonstrated; nominal reference builds are assumed.

paper: Security Analysis of Networked 3D Printers
attacks_mentioned: Tests a network-only adversary against 13 printers, demonstrating availability failures, spoofing opportunities, unauthenticated commands, malformed-input crashes, and exposed vulnerable services. It also models multistage paths through surrounding networks; these paths depend on assumed device compromises.
lifecycle_stage: S1/S2: unauthorized job access and design/command transfer; S3: printer control, availability, and network exposure during operation.
purdue_level: L5/L4 surrounding enterprise/site deployments where analyzed; L3 job/command transfer; L2 network-accessible printer services; L1 printer controller.
threat_model: Network-only adversary sends unauthenticated commands or malformed input, targets exposed services and availability, and may spoof devices. Wider multi-stage paths assume additional network/device compromises; stealth/evasion is outside study.

paper: Security Analysis of the 3MF Data Format
attacks_mentioned: An attacker distributes a malicious 3MF file that a victim application opens. XML/OPC parsing and inconsistent interpretation enable data exfiltration, denial of service, or different displayed models across applications, without preinstalled malware or network compromise.
lifecycle_stage: S1: intake/opening of untrusted model files; S2: model parsing and slicer preparation.
purdue_level: L5 enterprise model-file intake and application access; L3 model parsing and slicer preparation.
threat_model: Attacker supplies a malicious 3MF file that a victim opens, exploiting parsing or interpretation discrepancies for exfiltration, denial of service or cross-application model spoofing; no preinstalled malware or network compromise assumed.

paper: Security Challenges of Additive Manufacturing with Metals and Alloys
attacks_mentioned: Analyzes potential attacks through supply chains, firmware updates, malicious input files, model modification, and process specifications. Manipulating orientation, layer properties, heat delivery, timing, atmosphere, or postprocessing could degrade metal parts or damage equipment.
lifecycle_stage: S1: model intake/supply-chain trust; S2: orientation and process preparation; S3: machine parameters and atmosphere; S4: explicit postprocessing and cooling manipulation.
purdue_level: L5 file/supply-chain handling; L3 process/orientation preparation; L1–L0 machine, atmosphere and postprocessing equipment.
threat_model: Qualitative analysis considers malicious supply-chain actors, file/firmware manipulation and changed metal process or postprocessing settings to damage equipment or weaken parts; access and capability vary by scenario, with no single tested adversary.

paper: Security features embedded in computer aided design (CAD) solid models for additive manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Addresses unauthorized printing from stolen CAD designs, assuming the adversary lacks the legitimate processing recipe. It does not prevent file theft or demonstrate an intrusion.
lifecycle_stage: S1 design embeds protection; S2 conversion and slicing select the recipe; S3 fabrication realizes the conditional features.
purdue_level: L5 CAD design and access; L3 STL conversion, slicing and recipe; L1–L0 printing realizes embedded physical defects.
threat_model: Unauthorized manufacturer obtains protected CAD but lacks legitimate conversion, slicing and build parameters and seeks to print a sound counterfeit; no intrusion or prevention of file theft is demonstrated.

paper: Security Implications of Malicious G-Codes in 3D Printing
attacks_mentioned: Systematizes information disclosure, denial of service, and model manipulation through G-code, including limited access before a victim’s job, malicious slicer configuration, and runtime injection. Persistent settings can affect later jobs without modifying their complete toolpaths.
lifecycle_stage: S1/S2: untrusted job/configuration intake and preprint scanning; S3: printer configuration, command execution, and effects on subsequent prints.
purdue_level: L3 untrusted slicer/configuration and build files; L2 printer job/control interfaces and proposed scanning; L1 firmware/command execution; L0 physical printer effects where tested.
threat_model: An attacker with limited ability to submit G-code or change slicer settings injects malicious persistent commands before or during victim jobs, seeking data disclosure, denial of service or physical manipulation. Full firmware compromise is not required.

paper: Security of Additive Manufacturing: Attack Taxonomy and Survey
attacks_mentioned: Surveys technical-data theft and sabotage through compromised actors, files, software, firmware, networks and physical supplies. Its causal taxonomy connects access vectors, compromised elements, feasible manipulations, resulting effects and adversarial goals; it introduces no new attack experiment.
lifecycle_stage: S1–S5 review coverage spans design access, build preparation, fabrication, actual heat treatment/finish machining, and quality inspection. Coverage is analytical and bibliographic, not an experimentally secured end-to-end workflow.
purdue_level: Literature scope includes L5 enterprise design/supply chain, L3 preparation, L2–L0 execution, finishing and inspection. These are reviewed conceptual locations, not a demonstrated end-to-end secure architecture.
threat_model: Survey organizes adversary goals, access vectors, compromised components and manipulations across IP theft and sabotage; attacker capabilities vary by cited study. No single operational threat model or new attack experiment is claimed.

paper: Security of Cyber-Physical Additive Manufacturing Supply Chain: Survey, Attack Taxonomy and Solutions
attacks_mentioned: Surveys IP theft, unauthorized production, sabotage, data breaches and disruption across AM supply-chain activities. Examples include design/toolpath changes, material substitution and equipment manipulation. The aerospace company scenario is an illustrative attack narrative, not a verified incident or measured experiment.
lifecycle_stage: S1–S5 review scope includes design and procurement, preparation, manufacturing, actual surface/thermal postprocessing and quality checks. Distribution and returns extend beyond these AM production stages.
purdue_level: Literature spans L5–L4 design/procurement and authorization, L3 preparation, L2–L0 build, postprocessing and inspection.
threat_model: Survey considers insider/outsider IP theft, unauthorized production, sabotage, data breaches and disruption across AM supply chains. Access and capabilities vary across examples; aerospace scenario is illustrative, not an independently verified incident.

paper: See No Evil, Hear No Evil, Feel No Evil, Print No Evil? Malicious Fill Patterns Detection in Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: * Acoustic and spatial verification attack
lifecycle_stage: Printing
purdue_level: L1 firmware/controller and L0 physical printing/materials; L2 independent acoustic/spatial monitoring; L0/2 postproduction material inspection.
threat_model: Adversary can manipulate printer firmware or controller PC to change object specifications, manufacturing parameters or source materials; independent sensing is designed not to trust the printer's control stack.

paper: Side Channels of Cyber-Physical Systems: Case Study in Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Side-channel attacks
lifecycle_stage: Printing
purdue_level: L3 targeted G/M-code/geometry; L1 motor control and L0 process emissions measured during printing. This is a confidentiality case study, not a network compromise.
threat_model: Attacker learns side-channel mappings using known G/M-code and a similar printer, then observes target printer emissions to infer geometry. The source discusses acoustic, power, magnetic and vibration signals; the training and target access are attack assumptions.

paper: Simulating cyber-physical systems: Identifying vulnerabilities for design and manufacturing through simulated additive manufacturing environments
attacks_mentioned: Simulates a CAD-level internal pyramidal void that leaves external faces unchanged, then carries the altered design through slicing into a digital FFF build. This is an attack-effect simulation, not a machine-compromise demonstration.
lifecycle_stage: S1 design alteration and S2 slicing/simulation are represented, with S3 fabrication modeled and physically validated. S5 mass and dimensional inspection are explicitly assessed in simulation.
purdue_level: L5 design modification, L3 slicing and simulated G-code, L1–L0 physical/simulated printing and metrology. Inspection tests target part measurement, not proven network compromise.
threat_model: Assumes adversary can alter a CAD model by adding an internal void while keeping exterior unchanged. Attack propagation is simulated through slicing and printing; actual compromise path and attacker access are not demonstrated.

paper: SL1C3D: Slicer Library Injection for Covert 3D Data
attacks_mentioned: Demonstrates compromised PrusaSlicer libraries that embed covert character strokes in internal infill while displaying a benign preview. Library compromise is the starting assumption; the attack conceals changed G-code inside an apparently ordinary printed object.
lifecycle_stage: S2: slicer compromise, toolpath generation, and deceptive preview; S3: embedded infill execution.
purdue_level: L3 slicer library, toolpath and preview manipulation; L1–L0 printer execution and embedded infill.
threat_model: Attacker is assumed able to replace PrusaSlicer libraries; altered slicer embeds covert characters in infill/toolpath and shows benign preview. Aim is covert data embedding; initial library compromise is not demonstrated.

paper: SOK: 3D Printer Firmware Attacks on Fused Filament Fabrication
attacks_mentioned:
1. Object Geometry (OG) Stealing
2. Print Your Own Grave (PYOG) Attack
3. Incurable: Printing Faults Impersonation
4. Object Feature (OF) Scaling
5. Axial Misalignment
6. Internal Cavity Attack
7. Object Density Variation Attack
8. Filament Erosion Attack
9. Printing Facility Air-quality
lifecycle_stage: Design -> Slicing -> Printing
purdue_level: L5 CAD design context, L3 slicing/G-code, L1 compromised firmware and L0 printing, equipment and emissions.
threat_model: Assumes malicious firmware installed on an FFF printer; demonstrates nine attacks aiming at surveillance, denial of service and integrity harm to parts, printer or surroundings. The analysis compares 48 attacks across design, slicing and firmware placement.

paper: SoK: Identifying and Unifying Limitations, Security Threats & Vulnerabilities in Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Reviews technical-data theft and sabotage through software/firmware weaknesses, unprotected communications, side-channel leakage, geometry or parameter changes, and manipulated feedback. Targets include manufactured parts, equipment and the surrounding environment. Attacks and reported outcomes are drawn from cited studies, not new experiments.
lifecycle_stage: S1–S5 review scope spans design/data access, slicing and process planning, build execution, actual heat treatment/finishing, and finished-part inspection.
purdue_level: Literature spans L5 design and access, L3 slicing/preparation, and L2–L0 build, finishing and inspection.
threat_model: User-approved v3 survey synthesizes data theft and sabotage through access, communications, firmware, sensors and process changes. Attacker type, access and capabilities vary by cited study; it does not specify a single tested adversary.

paper: SoK: Side Channel Monitoring for Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Reviews malicious FFF-process deviations alongside ordinary quality defects, including geometry, extrusion, temperature, timing, and layer changes. Side-channel IP theft is contextual; the paper’s main focus is monitoring sabotage and process quality, not a new attack.
lifecycle_stage: Primarily S3: in-process sensing and anomaly detection. S2 reference models support reviewed methods;
purdue_level: Primarily L0 sensors/physical emissions and L2 monitoring/analysis; L1 process actuation and L3 trusted reference preparation where covered by surveyed methods.
threat_model: Survey covers malicious FFF process changes and benign defects, plus contextual IP side channels. Attacker access and capabilities vary across referenced studies; no single new threat model or attack is executed.

paper: Spatiotemporal G-code Modeling for Secure FDM-Based 3D Printing
attacks_mentioned: Evaluates sixteen classes of manipulated G-code affecting nozzle motion, filament kinetics, layer changes, timing, infill, and nozzle/bed temperature. Cyber access is assumed; attacks are enacted by changing instructions supplied to the printer.
lifecycle_stage: S2: trusted instruction transformation and parameter modeling; S3: independent sensing and layer-by-layer authentication during printing.
purdue_level: L3 trusted G-code and profile generation; L2 independent sensor acquisition/comparison; L1–L0 motor/temperature control and physical process.
threat_model: Attacker can change G-code before or during delivery to the printer and aims to perturb motion, filament, timing, infill or temperature. Detector assumes trusted G-code and independent calibrated sensing; initial cyber access is assumed.

paper: Spooky Manufacturing: Probabilistic Sabotage Attack in Metal Additive Manufacturing Using Shielding Gas Flow Control
venue: ACM CCS Workshop on Additive Manufacturing Security (AMSec@CCS); 2022
attacks_mentioned: Analyzes shielding-gas-flow sabotage in laser powder-bed fusion. Insufficient or excessive flow can affect laser attenuation, spatter deposition and powder uniformity, producing probabilistic defects in one or multiple parts. Candidate compromised controllers, sensors and supply-chain entry paths are reasoned, not exploited.
lifecycle_stage: S3: gas-flow control and associated build defects. S5 inspection and witness-coupon implications are discussed analytically
purdue_level: L1 gas-flow control and sensors; L0 gas, powder and physical build; L2–L0 inspection/witness-coupon implications are analytical.
threat_model: Conceptual adversary manipulates shielding-gas-flow controls, sensors or supply path to cause probabilistic LPBF defects. Initial compromise and exact access are hypothesized, not exploited; no measured success probability.

paper: State of Security Awareness in the Additive Manufacturing Industry: 2020 Survey
venue: ASTM STP 1644: Progress in Additive Manufacturing 2021; 2022
attacks_mentioned: Surveys perceived AM threats, adversaries, attacker objectives, outsourcing risks, and reported incidents. IP theft and sabotage are respondent/research concerns; the study neither executes attacks nor establishes their prevalence through independently verified incident data.
lifecycle_stage: S1: organizational risk planning, supplier/outsourcing trust, and security governance.
purdue_level: L5–L4 enterprise awareness, organizational risk and supplier governance.
threat_model: Questionnaire asks participants about perceived adversaries, IP theft, sabotage, outsourcing and incidents. It does not define or demonstrate a single attacker capability/access model or independently confirm incident reports.

paper: Stealthy Cyber Anomaly Detection On Large Noisy Multi-material 3D Printer Datasets Using Probabilistic Models
venue: ACM CCS Workshop on Additive Manufacturing Security (AMSec@CCS); 2022
attacks_mentioned: Emulates gradual temperature-setpoint changes and small single-command Z-axis changes in a fiber-reinforced polymer printer. Toolpath access is assumed; attack classes target subtle process deviations, and mechanical effects are not uniformly damaging.
lifecycle_stage: S2/S3: altered G-code and execution-side monitoring. Mechanical flex tests validate consequences rather than constituting an S5 security workflow;
purdue_level: L3 toolpath/parameter changes; L1–L0 temperature/Z control and process signals; L2 signal collection and probabilistic monitoring. Mechanical tests evaluate effects, not a deployed certification workflow.
threat_model: Attack emulation changes temperature setpoints or a single Z-axis instruction, assuming access to build commands, to produce subtle process deviations. Detector assumes known-good baseline and labeled attacked runs; no initial intrusion demonstrated.

paper: Streaming in Metal Additive Manufacturing: A Catalyst for Secure Distributed Manufacturing
venue: International Journal of Production Research (online 2025; vol. 64 issue 10 in 2026); 2025
attacks_mentioned: Considers theft and unauthorized reuse of metal-AM production data through interception, redirection, memory extraction and compromised machine software. These are analysed threat scenarios, not demonstrated penetration tests; software that copies decrypted layers can undermine the protection.
lifecycle_stage: S1 production authorization, S2 preparation of streamable build data and S3 layer delivery/execution.
purdue_level: L5 licensing/authorization and server/client collaboration; L3 prepared layer data and stream generation; L2–L1 client/controller layer delivery; L0 metal printer execution.
threat_model: Threat analysis considers theft, interception, redirection or memory extraction of production data during outsourced metal-AM manufacturing. Authenticated stream assumes trusted machine-side software and license management; a compromised client can copy decrypted workplanes.

paper: Survey of 3D Printer Security Offensive and Defensive
attacks_mentioned: Surveys attacks by intent: technical-data theft, AM sabotage and illegal-part manufacturing. Reviewed mechanisms include side-channel leakage, geometry/parameter tampering, firmware modification and material manipulation. Illegal manufacturing is explicitly distinguished from an external intrusion against a printer owner.
lifecycle_stage: S1–S3 scope includes data access, model/toolpath preparation and machine execution. S4 finishing appears in a cited workflow;
purdue_level: L5 design access, L3 preparation, L2–L0 execution and inspection as reviewed conceptual scope
threat_model: Survey classifies IP theft, sabotage and illegal manufacture; attacker access and capabilities differ across cited studies. Illegal printing is treated separately from outside compromise of the printer owner.

paper: Taxonomies for Reasoning About Cyber-physical Attacks in IoT-based Manufacturing Systems
venue: Int. J. Interact. Multim. Artif. Intell.; 2017
attacks_mentioned: Classifies manufacturing attacks by vectors, vulnerabilities, targets, and confidentiality/integrity/availability impacts, including material and geometric manipulation. Connects software vulnerabilities to possible manufacturing consequences; case-study paths are reasoned possibilities rather than demonstrated exploit chains.
lifecycle_stage: S1: customer design intake; S2: file preparation; S3: machine/process checks; S5: part inspection and vulnerable inspection systems.
purdue_level: L5 customer design intake; L3 build preparation; L2–L0 process control and quality inspection.
threat_model: Models possible attacks by vector, vulnerability, targets and impacts in an AM service-provider infrastructure, including compromised design, production and inspection computers. Access varies by scenario; paths are reasoned, not demonstrated exploit chains.

paper: Taxonomy-Driven Graph-Theoretic Framework for Manufacturing Cybersecurity Risk Modeling and Assessment
attacks_mentioned: Models possible manufacturing attacks as paths from entry vectors through affected locations to consequences. The illustrative manufacturing-as-a-service case considers hardware tampering and man-in-the-middle access affecting part quality; it does not execute these attacks.
lifecycle_stage: Conceptual S1 design intake, S2 production instructions, S3 machine operation and S5 dimensional inspection occur in the illustrative workflow.
purdue_level: L5 design/customer access, L3 manufacturing instruction preparation, L1–L0 machine hardware and part production,
threat_model: Illustrative manufacturing-as-a-service scenario models hardware tampering and man-in-the-middle attacks, assuming graph paths and numerical exploit/propagation probabilities; attackers seek part-quality impact. No intrusion is executed.

paper: Thermal Side-Channel Forensics in Additive Manufacturing Systems
attacks_mentioned: Side-channel attack -> THERMAL FORENSICS
lifecycle_stage: Printing
purdue_level: L0 thermal emissions during printing and L3 exposed digital instructions;
threat_model: An observer uses thermal images of additive manufacturing to infer printing parameters and potentially geometry; exact placement, access and reconstruction capabilities require the poster text.

paper: Threat modelling for industrial cyber physical systems in the era of smart manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Models industrial-control threats by linking actors, assets, vulnerabilities, attack techniques, and consequences. Attack trees and risk rankings are developed for a Festo automotive-production test rig, rather than demonstrated AM sabotage.
lifecycle_stage: General ICPS design and operation are covered. An AM-specific S1–S5 mapping is not established because the validation concerns an automotive test rig rather than an additive-manufacturing workflow.
purdue_level: General ICPS case concerns Festo automotive rig and associated engineering/control systems
threat_model: Threat modeling considers actors, vulnerabilities and industrial control-system consequences in an automotive production test rig; access varies by modeled attack tree. No AM-specific attack or attacker capabilities established.

paper: TMAP: A Threat Modeling and Attack Path Analysis Framework for Industrial IoT Systems (A Case Study of IoM and IoP)
venue: Arabian Journal for Science and Engineering; 2023
attacks_mentioned: Models spoofing, tampering, disclosure, denial of service and privilege escalation across IIoT assets and communications. Manufacturing HMI and electric-power SCADA cases illustrate attack paths; these are modeled possibilities, not executed intrusions.
lifecycle_stage: No AM lifecycle stage is established. The cases address general manufacturing and electric-power control systems, without an additive-manufacturing process demonstration.
purdue_level: not an AM demonstration.
threat_model: STRIDE-based IIoT modeling considers spoofing, tampering, information disclosure, denial of service and privilege escalation; manufacturing HMI and power SCADA attack paths are hypothetical, not executed. No AM-specific adversary established.

paper: Tool of Spies: Leaking Your Intellectual Property by Altering the Compiler
venue: IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing; 2019
attacks_mentioned: Assumes one-time access to alter the CAM compiler plus nearby sensing and profiling on the target or a similar printer. Compiler-inserted parameter changes amplify acoustic, vibration, electromagnetic or power leakage so an attacker can infer geometric instructions more easily.
lifecycle_stage: S2: compiler/toolpath preparation introduces leakage-enhancing instructions. S3: physical emissions are captured during fabrication to infer design information.
purdue_level: L3 compiler/toolpath preparation; L1 motor/firmware actuation; L0 physical emissions and nearby sensors.
threat_model: Attacker obtains one-time access to the CAM compiler and nearby sensing/profiling on the target or similar printer. Compiler-inserted parameter changes enhance acoustic, vibration, electromagnetic or power leakage to infer geometry.

paper: Turning Hearsay into Discovery: Industrial 3D Printer Side Channel Information Translated to Stealing the Object Design
attacks_mentioned: A malicious manufacturer or insider with physical access instruments laser current and galvanometer position-output voltages to reconstruct printed designs. Demonstrated on a Sintratec S2 polymer powder-bed-fusion machine; this is privileged internal measurement, not remote eavesdropping.
lifecycle_stage: S3: information leakage is captured during build execution. Design confidentiality is the protected asset;
purdue_level: L1 galvanometer/laser control outputs and L0 actuator signals/material process; recovered design is an L3 information asset.
threat_model: Malicious manufacturer/insider with privileged physical access instruments laser current and galvanometer position test points to reconstruct printed geometry. No remote eavesdropping is demonstrated; calibration and original STL dimensions are used in experimental correction.

paper: Using 3D printers as weapons
attacks_mentioned: Conceptually examines compromised AM workflows causing harmful physical effects through altered materials, object specifications, manufacturing parameters or postprocessing. Targets include parts, equipment and their environment. The authors explicitly characterize the attack examples as primarily hypothetical and requiring experimental or real-world confirmation.
lifecycle_stage: S1–S4 coverage includes supply/design access, object and process specifications, fabrication, and actual hot-isostatic-pressing/postprocessing parameters.
purdue_level: L5 supply/design; L3 object and process specifications; L1–L0 fabrication and postprocessing controls/physical process.
threat_model: Hypothetical attacker controls selected compromised workflow elements and manipulates materials, object specifications, processes or postprocessing to produce harmful parts, equipment or environmental outcomes. Coordinated attacks are outside the developed taxonomy.

paper: Vulnerabilities and Attacks on CAN-Based 3D Printing/Additive Manufacturing
attacks_mentioned: Assumes one compromised CAN node or a malicious replacement module. Unauthenticated shared traffic enables sniffing, spoofed commands and sensor feedback, and denial of service. A microcontroller on a commercial printer’s CAN hub injects false temperature reports, causing shutdown; additional control and safety manipulations are reported.
lifecycle_stage: S3: module initialization, machine calibration, sensor feedback and build-time actuation.
purdue_level: L1 CAN-connected controller/modules and shared control communications; L0 temperature sensor and physical printer; L2 operator-visible machine status where applicable.
threat_model: Attacker compromises or replaces a CAN node, or attaches a malicious device to a shared bus; unauthenticated traffic permits sniffing, spoofed commands/sensor feedback and denial of service. Temperature spoofing is demonstrated with physical bus access.

paper: Watching and Safeguarding Your 3D Printer: Online Process Monitoring Against Cyber-Physical Attacks
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies; 2018
